content.title: Computers Do Exactly What You Said
content.hook: Imagine giving a helper one instruction: “Put the cup on the table.” A person may fill in missing details from common sense. A computer does not have that same common sense. It follows the instructions available to it.
content.context: That is useful. It is also dangerous. A computer can perform an instruction perfectly and still give you the wrong result if the instruction was wrong.
goals: Understand that a computer follows the instructions it receives literally; when the result is wrong, the instruction itself must be examined.

content.question:
You tell a computer to repeat these steps exactly:

1. Start with 5.
2. Add 2.
3. Subtract 1.

What result should you expect?

feedback.correct: The machine does not need to “understand” the goal. It follows the listed steps: 5 → 7 → 6.
feedback.incorrect: The machine does not need to “understand” the goal. It follows the listed steps: 5 → 7 → 6.

content.question:
A learner wants a total of 10. They write these instructions:

1. Start with 4.
2. Add 3.
3. Add 1.

The computer produces 8. Did the computer make a mistake?

options.text: Yes. Computers should know the intended answer.
No. It followed the instructions; the instructions did not produce the intended result.
Only if the screen looked wrong.

feedback.correct: This is one of the most important engineering habits in Forge: separate “the computer did what I said” from “I said the right thing.”
feedback.incorrect: This is one of the most important engineering habits in Forge: separate “the computer did what I said” from “I said the right thing.”

content.question:
Keep the first two steps the same:

1. Start with 4.
2. Add 3.

You need the final answer to become 10. Which next instruction is enough?

feedback.correct: After step 2 the value is 7. Adding 3 gives 10. The important move is not guessing—it is checking the current result before choosing the next instruction.
feedback.incorrect: After step 2 the value is 7. Adding 3 gives 10. The important move is not guessing—it is checking the current result before choosing the next instruction.

content.title: The instruction test
content.text:
When a result surprises you, ask two different questions:

“Did the computer follow the instructions?”
“Did the instructions describe what I actually wanted?”

Those are different questions. Keeping them separate makes mistakes easier to investigate.

activities.title: Tiny exercise
activities.instruction: Compose your response below, then submit to compare with the reference guide.

content.prompt: Write a four-step set of plain-English instructions that starts at 2 and ends at 9. You may only add or subtract whole numbers.
guidelines: State your reasoning clearly in your own words or code.
Compare your response with the reference guide after submitting.
content.sampleResponse:
Start at 2 → add 4 → add 3 → add 0.

Many correct answers are possible. The goal is to make each step explicit enough that another person could follow it without guessing.

feedback.correct: Many correct answers are possible. The goal is to make each step explicit enough that another person could follow it without guessing.
feedback.incorrect: Please write a brief response (at least 10 characters) before submitting.

content.question: Which statement is the strongest engineering explanation?

options.text: “The result came from the instructions; I need to check the instructions against the result I wanted.”
“Try random changes until the output looks right.”

feedback.correct: Good problem solving starts with evidence and instructions, not random edits.
feedback.incorrect: Good problem solving starts with evidence and instructions, not random edits.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: Mental model: Computers are literal. They are excellent at carrying out instructions and terrible at guessing missing intent.
Senior habit: When the result is wrong, inspect the instructions before blaming the machine.
nextSteps: Complete the checkpoint and show the reasoning, not just the final answer. The goal is to build the habit of making a prediction, comparing evidence, and repairing the smallest justified step.

requirements: Screen-reader accessible code blocks and options
